# Pannun Case: Hague Service Convention Article 19 and Section 29 CPC on Service of Foreign Summons


US court order on summons to Indian officials in the Pannun civil case: Hague Service Convention Article 19, Section 29(c) CPC and Order V explained, with UPSC notes.


India And Usa


Nov, 2026


•


4 min read


### Overview


On 9 November 2026, US District Judge Katherine Polk Failla (Southern District of New York) allowed a request by Gurpatwant Singh Pannun to send summons to Ajit Doval and former RAW chief Samant Goel through Indian courts, under the Hague Service Convention. The suit is a civil case in which Pannun alleges a conspiracy to assassinate him in New York. The allegations are unproven (The Wire; The Print; Bar Bulletin).


## Why in the News: US Court Order on Service of Summons


According to the order dated 9 November 2026, Judge Failla allowed Pannun's request to send summons to Ajit Doval and former RAW chief Samant Goel. The summons would go through the US judiciary to the Indian courts that have jurisdiction over their addresses (The Wire; The Print; Bar Bulletin).


- The suit is a civil case. The plaintiff alleges a conspiracy to assassinate him in New York.
- The allegations are unproven. India has rejected such allegations.
- Earlier attempts at personal service and through India's Central Authority failed.

## The Legal Basis Cited by the Court


As reported, the court relied on the following:


- **Article 19 of the Hague Convention** on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents. It covers service through methods allowed by the destination country's domestic law.
- **Section 29(c) of India's Code of Civil Procedure (CPC).**
- **A January 2009 Indian notification** applying Section 29 to civil courts in Hague Convention countries.


The procedure referred to is Order V, Rules 21 and 23 of the CPC.


## What Happens Next: The 30 November Deadline


The court directed Pannun's lawyers to submit proposed documents by 30 November. The clerk may then forward them to Delhi courts (The Wire; The Print; Bar Bulletin).

## Mains Angle: International Law, Sovereign Immunity and India-US Relations


The case can be read through three themes. This section describes them in general terms and does not take a side on the dispute.


- **International law:** the Hague Service Convention sets out routes for serving court documents across borders, including methods allowed by the destination country's domestic law.
- **Sovereign immunity concerns:** the persons named are an Indian official and a former official, so questions of immunity can arise in this kind of suit. The sources reviewed here do not report a ruling on them.
- **India-US relations:** the case involves a US court and Indian courts and officials.


## Exam Relevance


Prelims: Article 19 of the Hague Service Convention, Section 29(c) and Order V of the CPC, and the January 2009 notification. Mains: GS-2 international relations and GS-2 judiciary, framed around cross-border service of documents and sovereign immunity.

## Key Takeaways


- On 9 November 2026, Judge Katherine Polk Failla allowed summons to be sent to Ajit Doval and Samant Goel through Indian courts.
- The court relied on Article 19 of the Hague Convention, Section 29(c) of the CPC and a January 2009 notification. The procedure is under Order V, Rules 21 and 23.
- Pannun's lawyers must submit proposed documents by 30 November.
- The allegations are unproven.
